passage: Note by Jagdish, mentor. On Monday Rashmi showed me two messages she had sent through a professional network, one to an engineer at each firm that had offered her a job. Each asked the same three things: how heavy the workload gets, how much people learn, and how appraisals work. By Wednesday both had replied. One wrote that sprints end late on Thursdays, learning is mostly on your own, and appraisal comes once a year. The other described weekly code reviews, a small course budget, and appraisal every six months. Rashmi copied both answers into a table. "None of this was in the offer letters," she said. I suggested nothing. She will ask each HR team about appraisal timing before Friday.

qa.a: She could ask each HR team the same questions in writing, because two individual views may be a little biased and an official reply is easier to compare.

qa.q: How might Jagdish see Rashmi's approach?
qa.a: Jagdish watches a graduate collecting facts before choosing, and holds back suggestions so that the decision stays with Rashmi.

subtype: Approach: talking to current employees at both firms [Action]
passage:
Thursday
Did the thing I was scared of: messaged strangers.
Found two people on the professional networking site: Zeenat, a junior analyst at the insurance company for a year, and Rohit, at the fintech start-up for eight months. Short messages: who I am, which offer, could I ask three questions in 15 minutes?
Both said yes!
Same three questions to each: What's a normal week's workload? What have you learned in your first year? How do appraisals really work?
Zeenat: 9 to 6, rarely later; formal training for three months; appraisal once a year, clear ratings.
Rohit: honest guy. Said 50-hour weeks are normal, learning is huge but self-taught, and appraisals "happen when the founder remembers."
None of this was in either offer letter.
I don't know yet which I'll pick. But now I'm choosing between two real jobs, not two PDFs.
Bhavna

qa.q: How long has Zeenat been at the insurance company?
qa.a: Zeenat has been a junior analyst there for a year.

qa.q: How did Bhavna feel about messaging strangers?
qa.a: Bhavna was scared at first, then thrilled when both said yes.

qa.q: What else could Bhavna ask before deciding?
qa.a: Bhavna could ask each company's HR to confirm training and appraisal details in writing, to check what the employees said.

qa.q: How might Rohit see Bhavna's questions?
qa.a: Rohit seems glad to be honest, sharing the long weeks and loose appraisals so a newcomer knows what to expect.

grounding: Shows a graduate contacting current employees at both firms, asking about workload, learning and appraisals, and hearing what the offer letters left out.

Ritu: hi Aparna, thanks for accepting! I have an offer from your company for the junior design role. could I ask a few things?
Aparna: sure, happy to
Ritu: what's the workload like in a normal week?
Aparna: honestly depends on the client. usually around 45 hrs, launch weeks more
Ritu: and do juniors get to learn from seniors?
Aparna: yes, we have a weekly critique where seniors review everyone's work. that's the best part
Ritu: how do appraisals work? the letter just says "annual review"
Aparna: reviews twice a year actually, with a written feedback form. raises only once a year though
Ritu: that's really useful. the letter didn't mention the critique at all
Aparna: letters never do 😄 talk to someone at your other offer too, so you're comparing like with like
Ritu: already messaged someone there. thank you so much 🙏

qa.q: How often are reviews at Aparna's company?
qa.a: Twice a year, with a written feedback form.

qa.q: How does Ritu seem to feel after the chat?
qa.a: Ritu feels grateful and better informed, relieved to learn details like the weekly critique that the letter left out.

qa.q: What else could Ritu ask the person at the other company?
qa.a: Ritu could ask the same three questions, so the answers from both firms can be compared fairly.

qa.q: How does Aparna see Ritu's questions?
qa.a: Aparna is happy to help and even advises comparing like with like, knowing that offer letters never tell the full story.

grounding: Illustrates a graduate asking a current employee about workload, learning and appraisals and getting details missing from the offer letter.
